From an inference result to a grain plan

Source: vignettes/grainplan.Rmd
grainplan.Rmd
library(grainPlan)
have_agridat <- requireNamespace("agridat", quietly = TRUE)
have_ggplot2 <- requireNamespace("ggplot2", quietly = TRUE)

Why

An agronomist closing out a season has three inference results waiting on the desk – a nitrogen-response trial, a variety trial, a protein target – and one blunt question for each: what should I actually do about it, and how do I tell when the tool itself does not trust the evidence enough to answer? A wrong number costs a season’s margin; a confident wrong number is worse than a plain shrug, because nobody double-checks a number that looks sure of itself.

grainPlan is the practitioner last-mile of the ORCHESTRA agricultural analytics stack. An upstream member produces an inference result – a yield posterior, a multi-environment variety trial, a genomic prediction – and grainPlan turns it into an actionable grain-production plan: how much nitrogen to apply, which variety to sow, whether to chase a quality grade. It is a thin grain-semantics layer over the decideR decision engine: the expected-utility maximisation, the abstention logic, and the grounding firewall are all decideR’s, reused whole; grainPlan adds the grain economics and the grain meaning. This walkthrough runs end-to-end on real public data from the agridat package and answers the agronomist’s question three times over – a rate, a variety, a grade target – and then a fourth time for the case a report cannot afford to get wrong: what the plan looks like when one of its legs is not there to trust.

What

Four decision verbs and two orchestrating types carry the whole of this vignette. plan_nitrogen_rate() and plan_nitrogen_rate_from_manifest() price a nitrogen rate by expected profit; plan_variety() and plan_variety_from_manifest() rank a candidate variety or hybrid under a downside-aware merit loss; plan_grade_target() chooses how hard to push a quality-driving input under a payoff that steps at a delivery-grade threshold. Every one of these wraps decideR::decide() or a sibling engine call and returns a grain_decision: the recommended action, its unit, a grower-facing rationale, and a grounding token copied straight off the wrapped decideR::decision, never recomputed. plan_season() gathers several grain_decisions into one grain_plan, combining their grounding worst-case through decideR::combine_grounding() so a plan resting on any unverified decision is itself unverified; grain_plan_table() flattens that plan into the one-row-per-decision table a report reads, and grain_is_grounded() is the predicate a downstream automation gates on before acting. The grain value library – wheat_protein_bands(), barley_malting_premium(), n_rate_economics() – consolidates the economics these decisions price against, so a schedule is named and documented rather than an anonymous expression re-derived at every call site.

Do

A nitrogen rate from a real yield response

The agridat dataset lasrosas.corn records corn yield-monitor data for a field near Las Rosas, Rio Cuarto, Cordoba, Argentina, under variable nitrogen fertiliser across the 1999 and 2001 harvests (Anselin, Bongiovanni & Lowenberg-DeBoer, 2004). We summarise it into a yield-response curve, build a posterior of yield at each candidate rate, and ask grainPlan for the profit-optimal rate. The economics live in the grain value library: n_rate_economics() consolidates the profit utility – revenue at the grain price less the nitrogen cost – so a profit-priced rate decision reads as its economics rather than as an anonymous expression.

data("lasrosas.corn", package = "agridat")
corn <- lasrosas.corn

# A candidate nitrogen grid spanning the trial, and a simple yield-response
# summary: a quadratic mean-yield fit against nitrogen, with the trial's
# residual spread used to build a posterior of yield at each rate. This
# stands in for the yield posterior an ORCHESTRA inference member (a PESTO
# inversion, a mechanistic yield-response model) would emit as an
# orchestra_manifest.
#
# The draws MUST be coupled across rate columns: one draw index has to mean
# "the same realised season" at every candidate rate, because the decision
# is a paired comparison between candidate rates on the posterior, not a
# comparison of two independent samples. We therefore draw one residual
# vector `eps` and add it to every rate's fitted mean, rather than drawing
# each column independently (independent columns roughly double the
# between-rate contrast variance and can mask a real, decisive difference).
rates <- seq(0, 120, by = 20)
fit <- stats::lm(yield ~ nitro + I(nitro^2), data = corn)
sigma <- summary(fit)$sigma

n_draws <- 1500L
eps <- stats::rnorm(n_draws, 0, sigma)
yield_draws <- vapply(
  rates,
  function(r) {
    mu <- stats::predict(fit, newdata = data.frame(nitro = r))
    mu + eps
  },
  numeric(n_draws))

# Grain and nitrogen prices are the caller's to supply. `lasrosas.corn`
# reports yield in quintals/ha (agridat's own documentation), so the grain
# price below is expressed per quintal; it is illustrative, not the price
# structure the trial's own economic analyses used (Anselin et al. (2004)
# report $6.85/quintal and $0.4348/kg N for their own analysis).
n_plan <- plan_nitrogen_rate(
  yield_draws, rates,
  price_grain = 22,             # $ per quintal (illustrative)
  price_n = 1.2,                # $ per unit nitrogen (illustrative)
  crop = "corn",
  grounding = decideR::grounding_grounded())

n_plan
#> <grain_decision> RECOMMENDED  [grounded]
#>   crop   : corn
#>   kind   : nitrogen_rate
#>   action : 80 kg N/ha
#>   why    : Apply 80 kg N/ha to the corn crop: it maximises expected profit ($1478.3/unit area) and clearly beats the status quo on the posterior.

The recommendation is a grain_decision: the chosen rate, the crop, a grower-facing rationale, and – carried beside the numbers, never inferred from them – the grounding token.

plot_df <- n_plan@decision@candidates
plot_df$role <- "candidate"
plot_df$role[plot_df$action == 0] <- "status quo"
plot_df$role[plot_df$action == n_plan@action] <- "chosen rate"
plot_df$role <- factor(plot_df$role,
                       levels = c("candidate", "status quo", "chosen rate"))

ggplot2::ggplot(plot_df, ggplot2::aes(x = action, y = expected_utility)) +
  ggplot2::geom_line(colour = "grey50") +
  ggplot2::geom_point(ggplot2::aes(colour = role, shape = role), size = 3) +
  ggplot2::scale_colour_manual(
    name = NULL,
    values = c(candidate = "#000000", `status quo` = "#0072B2",
               `chosen rate` = "#D55E00")) +
  ggplot2::scale_shape_manual(
    name = NULL,
    values = c(candidate = 16, `status quo` = 15, `chosen rate` = 17)) +
  ggplot2::labs(
    x = "Nitrogen rate (kg N/ha)", y = "Expected profit ($/unit area)",
    title = "Profit-vs-rate curve behind the recommendation") +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal()

Expected profit against candidate nitrogen rate for the lasrosas.corn fit: profit rises from the status quo, peaks at the chosen rate, and falls away beyond it.

The curve is why the decision is decisive rather than a coin toss between neighbouring rates: expected profit rises steadily from the status quo, peaks sharply at the chosen rate, and falls away either side of it, so the gap between the chosen rate and its nearest neighbours is well above the posterior’s rate-to-rate noise.

The firewall: unverified evidence abstains

Now the decisive behaviour. If the yield evidence is not grounded – the upstream producer did not verify it against an external authority – the same decision must not be made. grainPlan inherits decideR’s Independent Oracle Principle firewall: an unverified input forces abstention to the status-quo rate, never a confident wrong recommendation.

n_plan_unverified <- plan_nitrogen_rate(
  yield_draws, rates,
  price_grain = 22, price_n = 1.2, crop = "corn",
  grounding = decideR::grounding_unverified())

n_plan_unverified
#> <grain_decision> ABSTAINED  [ungrounded]
#>   crop   : corn
#>   kind   : nitrogen_rate
#>   action : 0 kg N/ha
#>   why    : Held at the status-quo rate: the yield evidence is unverified, so the Independent Oracle Principle firewall declines to act on it.

The only thing that changed between this call and the one above is the grounding token, and it flipped decide into abstain. This is the firewall a real grain tool needs: a nitrogen rate carries a cost in the paddock, so an unverified yield model is held at the status quo, not acted on.

A variety choice from a multi-environment trial

The agridat dataset besag.met is a multi-environment trial of 64 corn hybrids across six counties in North Carolina, with three replicates each (Besag & Higdon, 1999). We summarise each hybrid’s mean performance across counties into a posterior of merit, and ask grainPlan to rank them under a downside-aware loss – one that discounts a high-yielding but volatile hybrid against a steady one, the stability a grower wants from a sown variety.

data("besag.met", package = "agridat")
met <- besag.met

# Hybrid means across counties, with the county-to-county spread giving each
# hybrid a merit posterior. (A factor-analytic MET model --
# flexyBayes -- would emit this directly as an orchestra_manifest;
# here we build it directly from the public trial.) The posterior we need
# is of the HYBRID MEAN, not of a single plot, so the per-hybrid plot-level
# spread must be divided down to a standard error of the mean
# (sd / sqrt(n)); using the raw plot-level sd would overstate the mean's
# uncertainty by roughly sqrt(n) and could mask a real, decisive ranking.
# The trial ships with 36 filler rows (six per county) carrying a missing
# yield -- agridat's own note explains they complete the field rectangle for
# a spatial model and were never harvested -- so we summarise with na.rm and
# fall back to the trial-wide spread (also converted to a standard error)
# for any hybrid with too few records to estimate its own.
gen_means <- tapply(met$yield, met$gen, mean, na.rm = TRUE)
gen_sd <- tapply(met$yield, met$gen, stats::sd, na.rm = TRUE)
gen_n <- tapply(met$yield, met$gen, function(x) sum(!is.na(x)))
pooled_sd <- stats::sd(met$yield, na.rm = TRUE)
gen_sd[is.na(gen_sd)] <- pooled_sd
gen_n[gen_n < 2L] <- 1L
gen_se <- gen_sd / sqrt(gen_n)
varieties <- names(gen_means)

merit_draws <- vapply(
  seq_along(gen_means),
  function(j) stats::rnorm(1000L, gen_means[j], gen_se[j]),
  numeric(1000L))
colnames(merit_draws) <- varieties

v_plan <- plan_variety(
  merit_draws, varieties, risk_aversion = 0.5, crop = "corn",
  grounding = decideR::grounding_grounded())

v_plan
#> <grain_decision> RECOMMENDED  [grounded]
#>   crop   : corn
#>   kind   : variety
#>   action : G05 variety
#>   why    : Sow G05 in the corn crop: it leads the downside-aware merit ranking and clearly beats the incumbent (G01) on the posterior.

The recommendation is the leading hybrid on the downside-aware ranking; the full ranked short-list is in the wrapped decision’s candidate ledger, with the hybrid labels attached (the ledger’s action column carries the integer index grainPlan decides over, so we join the hybrid names back on for a readable table):

ledger <- v_plan@decision@candidates
ledger$hybrid <- varieties[ledger$action]
ledger <- ledger[order(-ledger$expected_utility),
                 c("hybrid", "action", "expected_utility", "feasible")]
The five leading corn hybrids on the downside-aware merit ranking.
Hybrid Index Expected merit Feasible
G05 5 119.98 TRUE
G54 54 119.85 TRUE
G38 38 117.95 TRUE
G61 61 116.59 TRUE
G22 22 114.87 TRUE

A quality-grade decision

Many grain payoffs are not smooth in the outcome they reward: a delivery is paid by quality grade, so the value steps at a protein threshold rather than rising continuously. grainPlan’s value library consolidates these grade schedules. wheat_protein_bands() prices the Australian milling-wheat grades by protein, following the band thresholds published by Grain Trade Australia, and plan_grade_target() decides how hard to push a protein-driving input under that step payoff – a decision governed by the posterior probability of clearing each band, exactly the threshold economics decideR’s grade-band loss expresses.

protein_value <- wheat_protein_bands()
Wheat protein-band payoffs (wheat_protein_bands() defaults; dollar values are illustrative, the band shape follows Grain Trade Australia’s published thresholds).
Band Payoff ($/tonne)
Feed (<10.5) 300
ASW [10.5, 11.5) 330
APW [11.5, 13.0) 360
AH/APH (>=13.0) 400 
grid_protein <- seq(9, 14, by = 0.02)
schedule_df <- data.frame(
  protein = grid_protein,
  payoff = protein_value(grid_protein))
breaks_df <- data.frame(protein = attr(protein_value, "breaks"))

ggplot2::ggplot(schedule_df, ggplot2::aes(x = protein, y = payoff)) +
  ggplot2::geom_step(colour = "#0072B2", linewidth = 0.9) +
  ggplot2::geom_vline(data = breaks_df, ggplot2::aes(xintercept = protein),
                       linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  ggplot2::labs(
    x = "Grain protein (%)", y = "Payoff ($/tonne)",
    title = "Wheat protein-band value schedule") +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal()

The wheat protein-band value schedule (wheat_protein_bands()): a price per tonne that steps up at each published grade threshold. Dashed lines mark the milling/hard/prime-hard breaks; the step shape is what the table above cannot show.

A baseline protein posterior just below the milling band, and a nitrogen top-up that lifts protein at a per-unit cost, gives grainPlan something to weigh against that schedule: the decision prices the chance of clearing the 11.5% band against the cost of pushing for it.

protein <- stats::rnorm(2000L, mean = 11.0, sd = 0.5)
g_plan <- plan_grade_target(
  protein, actions = seq(0, 60, by = 10), value = protein_value,
  quality_shift = function(rate, p) p + 0.02 * rate, cost = 0.3,
  crop = "wheat", grounding = decideR::grounding_grounded())

g_plan
#> <grain_decision> RECOMMENDED  [grounded]
#>   crop   : wheat
#>   kind   : grade_target
#>   action : 60 input level
#>   why    : Set the input to 60 for the wheat crop: it maximises the expected graded payoff ($341.41/t) by raising the posterior probability of clearing a higher quality band, net of input cost.

At this cost the top-up pays for itself: the recommended input level is the top of the candidate range, because the expected graded payoff rises monotonically with the higher probability of clearing the 11.5% band – the candidate ledger below shows the full trade-off.

Full candidate ledger behind the grade-target recommendation.
Input level Expected payoff ($/t) Feasible
0 329.88 TRUE
10 332.70 TRUE
20 335.35 TRUE
30 338.14 TRUE
40 340.10 TRUE
50 340.86 TRUE
60 341.41 TRUE

From an upstream manifest

The examples so far assembled the yield and merit posteriors by hand. In the orchestra, an upstream member emits an orchestra_manifest instead – the C2 v2 generic manifest contract in the orchestra’s cross-package governance – and grainPlan reads it directly through decideR’s duck-typed pipeline tail, taking no dependency on the manifest constructor package. Here is a minimal stand-in built from a tiny S7 class, standing for the manifest a real producer would emit.

mini_manifest <- S7::new_class(
  "mini_manifest",
  properties = list(
    outputs         = S7::class_any,
    metadata        = S7::class_list,
    run_id          = S7::class_character,
    emitter_package = S7::class_character))

A yield-per-rate draws matrix, the shape a PESTO inversion emits, carried in outputs with the producer’s grounding token in metadata$grounding:

rates_m <- seq(0, 150, by = 25)
ymax    <- stats::rnorm(1200L, 5.5, 0.3)
yld_m   <- vapply(rates_m,
                  function(r) 3 + (ymax - 3) * (1 - exp(-r / 80)),
                  numeric(1200L))
ym <- mini_manifest(outputs = yld_m,
                    metadata = list(grounding = decideR::grounding_grounded()))

plan_nitrogen_rate_from_manifest(ym, rates_m, price_grain = 350, price_n = 1.3,
                                 crop = "wheat")
#> <grain_decision> RECOMMENDED  [grounded]
#>   crop   : wheat
#>   kind   : nitrogen_rate
#>   action : 150 kg N/ha
#>   why    : Apply 150 kg N/ha to the wheat crop: it maximises expected profit ($1593/unit area) and clearly beats the status quo on the posterior.

The genomic tail reads breeding values the same way. A breeding_values manifest carries point GEBVs in outputs$gebv alongside their genomic uncertainty, so the reconstruction uses the genotypes’ own reliability rather than an invented spread.

gm <- mini_manifest(
  outputs  = list(gebv = c(Scepter = 0.2, Vixen = 1.1, Calibre = -0.3),
                  pev  = c(0.04, 0.04, 0.04)),
  metadata = list(grounding = decideR::grounding_grounded()))

g_dec <- plan_variety_from_manifest(gm, risk_aversion = 0.5)
g_dec
#> <grain_decision> RECOMMENDED  [grounded]
#>   crop   : wheat
#>   kind   : variety
#>   action : Vixen variety
#>   why    : Sow Vixen in the wheat crop: it leads the downside-aware merit ranking and clearly beats the incumbent (Scepter) on the posterior.
g_dec@context$gebv_sd_source
#> [1] "manifest_pev"

If a point-GEBV manifest carries no uncertainty and no gebv_sd is supplied, grainPlan stops rather than fabricate a scale for the reconstruction: a genotype switch must not turn on a magic constant.

gm_no_sd <- mini_manifest(
  outputs  = list(gebv = c(Scepter = 0.2, Vixen = 1.1, Calibre = -0.3)),
  metadata = list(grounding = decideR::grounding_grounded()))

plan_variety_from_manifest(gm_no_sd, risk_aversion = 0.5)
#> Error:
#> ! manifest carries point GEBVs with no per-genotype uncertainty (`pev`, `gebv_se`, or `reliability` + `genetic_var`) and `gebv_sd` was not supplied. Pass `gebv_sd` on the GEBV scale, or provide a manifest that carries the genomic uncertainty -- grainPlan will not fabricate it.

The stop is not a bug to route around: it is the same firewall discipline as the grounding token, applied to a different way an upstream producer’s claim can be too thin to act on.

A manifest can also carry a refusal of its own. When the upstream producer declares, in its own summary slot, that it did not produce a usable result – a PESTO ensemble that never converged, say – grainPlan reads that typed abstention before it ever looks at the draws, and holds the decision at the status quo regardless of what the (declined) manifest happens to carry:

refused_manifest <- mini_manifest(
  outputs = list(),
  metadata = list(
    grounding = decideR::grounding_grounded(),
    summary = list(headline = "no stable fit found", abstained = TRUE)),
  run_id = "demo-refused-01", emitter_package = "PESTO")

gd_refused <- plan_nitrogen_rate_from_manifest(
  refused_manifest, rates_m, price_grain = 350, price_n = 1.3, crop = "corn")

gd_refused
#> <grain_decision> ABSTAINED  [ungrounded]
#>   crop   : corn
#>   kind   : nitrogen_rate
#>   action : 0 kg N/ha
#>   why    : Held at the status-quo rate: the upstream evidence producer itself declined to produce a result, so the recommendation is withheld.

Note that the producer’s own grounding token claimed grounded; grainPlan never reaches it, because the typed abstention is checked first. The returned object also carries a class stamp a fleet-level gate can read without knowing it came from grainPlan specifically:

class(gd_refused)
#> [1] "orchestra_refusal"         "grainPlan_abstention"     
#> [3] "grainPlan::grain_decision" "S7_object"

grainPlan_abstention and orchestra_refusal are prepended ahead of grainPlan::grain_decision, the naming convention the orchestra’s cross-member decline gate reads producer-agnostically – a downstream automation recognises this as a refused decision without special-casing grainPlan’s own class.

Composing a season plan

Finally, the orchestrator. plan_season() gathers several grain decisions into one grain_plan whose grounding is the worst case across its decisions – a plan that rests on any unverified decision is itself unverified, the firewall applied one level up. A plan with a declined component is flagged so a report never reads a confident headline over it.

The nitrogen and variety decisions above come from two separate real trials – a precision-agriculture nitrogen trial in Argentina and a multi-environment hybrid trial in North Carolina – composed here only to show the orchestrator mechanics; a real season plan would draw both decisions from the one field. Because both trials happen to be corn, the plan below labels its crop explicitly rather than infer it from either input, so the composition is always unambiguous.

season <- plan_season(
  list(v_plan, n_plan),
  crop = "corn", season = "2026 demonstration")

season
#> <grain_plan> 2026 demonstration -- 2 decisions  [grounded]
#>   - [decide  ] variety       : G05 variety
#>   - [decide  ] nitrogen_rate : 80 kg N/ha
season_tbl <- grain_plan_table(season)
The season plan flattened for a report (plan grounding: grounded).
Decision Action Unit Abstained Grounding
variety G05 variety FALSE grounded
nitrogen_rate 80 kg N/ha FALSE grounded

Every recommendation in the plan carries its grounding, and the plan as a whole carries the worst case – so a grower, or a downstream automation, can gate on grain_is_grounded() before acting.

grain_is_grounded(season)
#> [1] TRUE

Both decisions above were grounded, so the plan reads clean end to end. That is the easy case. The harder, more consequential case is what happens when one leg of the season inherits a refusal from further upstream – the gd_refused decision built two sections back, standing in for a PESTO ensemble that never converged. Composed alongside the same variety decision, into a plan for the same crop:

season_refusal <- plan_season(
  list(v_plan, gd_refused),
  crop = "corn",
  season = "2026 demonstration -- nitrogen evidence withheld upstream")

season_refusal
#> <grain_plan> 2026 demonstration -- nitrogen evidence withheld upstream -- 2 decisions  [ungrounded]  (partial abstention)
#>   - [decide  ] variety       : G05 variety
#>   - [ABSTAIN ] nitrogen_rate : 0 kg N/ha
refusal_tbl <- grain_plan_table(season_refusal)
The same report over a season where the nitrogen leg inherits an upstream producer refusal (plan grounding: ungrounded).
Decision Action Unit Abstained Grounding
variety G05 variety FALSE grounded
nitrogen_rate 0 kg N/ha TRUE ungrounded 
grain_is_grounded(season_refusal)
#> [1] FALSE

Read

For the lasrosas.corn fit, grainPlan recommends 80 kg N/ha, at an expected profit of $1478.3 per unit area, against a status-quo profit of $1412.7 – the profit gain the figure shows as the gap between the vermillion point and the blue square. The recommendation carries the grounded token, so it is the number a grower acts on.

On the same trial, the leading hybrid is G05, with an expected downside-aware merit of 119.98; the short-list table carries every hybrid the ranking considered, in order.

For the protein target, the top-up pays for itself at every rate up to the top of the candidate grid: grainPlan recommends an input level of 60, at an expected graded payoff of $341.41 per tonne.

The first season plan carries 2 decisions, both decided, and a plan-level grounding of grounded: grain_is_grounded() returns TRUE, so a downstream gate lets the whole plan through. The second season plan carries the same variety decision beside the withheld nitrogen decision; its Abstained column reads TRUE for the nitrogen row and its Action column carries 0 kg N/ha – the status-quo fallback, not a priced recommendation – while the variety row is untouched. The plan’s own grounding drops to ungrounded and grain_is_grounded() returns FALSE. A report built on grain_plan_table() reads exactly those two columns, Abstained and Grounding, to decide how to render each row: a row with Abstained = TRUE is greyed out and printed as a declined recommendation carrying only its status-quo fallback, never presented beside a genuine number as though it were one.

That answers the agronomist’s question on all four counts: a rate, a hybrid, and a grade target when the evidence is grounded, and a plain, legible refusal – not a confident number – when a leg of the season is not there to trust.

Limits

The dollar values throughout – the nitrogen prices, the protein-band payoffs, the malting premium the vignette does not exercise – are illustrative and not current market prices or GRDC-origin figures; a real decision needs the caller’s own price sheet. The nitrogen-response fit pools both recorded harvest years (1999 and 2001) without a year effect, so the response curve is an average across two seasons rather than one season’s economics, and the season-composition examples draw their two decisions from two real but unrelated trials – an Argentine precision-agriculture strip trial and a North Carolina hybrid trial – to demonstrate the orchestrator’s mechanics, not to stand in for one grower’s actual paddock. plan_season() in this release composes by sequencing and worst-case grounding only: it does not re-optimise jointly across decisions, so a season plan is the sum of its parts, not a jointly optimal allocation across them. The grounding firewall itself trusts the token a caller or an upstream manifest supplies; grainPlan, like decideR, does not independently re-verify a producer’s claim of grounded against an external authority, it only propagates and combines the token worst-case – so a producer that mislabels its own evidence would still ride through, and the firewall protects only against evidence that declares its own unverified or abstained status, not evidence that misrepresents it.

What to read next

Getting started with decideR walks the expected-utility engine, the abstention logic and the grounding firewall from the ground up – every verb in this vignette wraps that engine rather than reimplementing it.

Reproduce

Seed 1L, set once at the top of this file; every draw in every section follows deterministically from that one stream.
